clinical_knowledge.topic: Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV pharyngitis) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV pharyngitis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management follows an evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for infectious mononucleosis (EBV pharyngitis), with streptococcal pharyngitis as a key differential, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe sore throat, high fever, swollen neck lumps, and exhaustion for 5 days

Key HPI features: 20M college student presents with 5 days of severe sore throat, fever of 38.8C, painful swollen lymph nodes in his neck, and profound fatigue. Reports being unable to attend classes due to exhaustion.
Objective/Exam findings: Fever 38.8C, exudative pharyngitis, tender bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal exam.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV pharyngitis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Streptococcal pharyngitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe abdominal pain — could suggest splenic enlargement/rupture risk.
management_principles: Perform rapid strep test and monospot (heterophile antibody) test to distinguish from streptococcal pharyngitis
Check for hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal exam given splenic rupture risk
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with severe sore throat, high fever, swollen neck lumps, and exhaustion for 5 days. 20M college student presents with 5 days of severe sore throat, fever of 38.8C, painful swollen lymph nodes in his neck, and profound fatigue. Reports being unable to attend classes due to exhaustion.
reference_soap.objective: Fever 38.8C, exudative pharyngitis, tender bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal exam.
reference_soap.assessment: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV pharyngitis), with streptococcal pharyngitis as the key differential to exclude.
reference_soap.plan: Perform rapid strep test and monospot (heterophile antibody) test. Check for hepatosplenomegaly. Recommend rest, hydration, avoidance of contact sports for 4 weeks (splenic rupture risk), and supportive care. Refer to specialty team if severe abdominal pain, airway compromise, or diagnostic uncertainty.

teaching.one_liner: Epstein-Barr virus infection causing severe sore throat, fever, tender swollen lymph nodes, and profound fatigue — needs a monospot test and strep testing, since the two can look similar.
red_flags: Severe abdominal pain — could suggest splenic enlargement/rupture risk

exam.finding: Young male appearing fatigued and mildly flushed, sitting comfortably without respiratory distress, stridor, or drooling.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 98 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 38.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Marked bilateral tonsillar enlargement and pharyngeal erythema with thick white exudates; uvula is midline with no peritonsillar bulging.
Prominent tender bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, along with mildly enlarged tender anterior cervical nodes.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender throughout with no guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness.
No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly palpable below the costal margins.
No erythematous rash, petechiae, or scarlatiniform sandpaper texture noted on the trunk or extremities.
